question: What is a blood antigen?

options.A: A fluid part of plasma that clots blood
options.B: A protein marker on red blood cells
options.C: A medication given during blood transfusion
options.D: A white blood cell that fights infection

explanation: Antigens are chemical markers sitting on the surface of red blood cells that the immune system uses to identify the blood type. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why does the body's immune system attack mismatched blood?

options.A: It tries to repair the damaged cells using white blood cells
options.B: It recognizes the foreign antigens as nonself and makes antibodies
options.C: It runs out of normal plasma proteins to handle the extra fluid
options.D: It mistakes the red blood cells for harmful bacteria

explanation: You've got this! The immune system's main job is spotting foreign invaders. When it sees unfamiliar antigens on donated red blood cells, it treats them as dangerous and attacks. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: What antibodies are found in the plasma of a person with Type AB blood?
explanation: Type AB blood has both A and B antigens on the cells, so the body does not make antibodies against either one, or it would attack its own blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient has Type A blood. What type of antibodies circulate in their plasma?
explanation: People with Type A blood have A antigens on their cells, so their immune system develops anti-B antibodies to fight off foreign B-type blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: When does an Rh-negative person usually develop anti-Rh antibodies?

options.A: After direct exposure to Rh-positive blood
options.B: Only after multiple pregnancies regardless of blood type
options.C: Naturally during the first few weeks of life
options.D: Before birth while inside the womb

explanation: Remember, unlike ABO antibodies which are present naturally, Rh antibodies only form after the immune system has its first contact with Rh-positive cells. Great job learning this! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What makes a person's blood type classified as Rh-positive?

options.A: The lack of any proteins on the cell surface
options.B: The presence of anti-Rh antibodies in the plasma
options.C: The presence of the D antigen on red blood cells
options.D: The ability to donate blood to anyone safely

explanation: The main determinant of Rh-positive status is finding the D antigen on the surface of the red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why do we perform a crossmatch test before giving a blood transfusion?

options.A: To check for direct reactions between donor cells and recipient serum
options.B: To measure the exact volume of red blood cells in the patient
options.C: To find out if the patient has any hidden infectious diseases
options.D: To determine the patient's baseline hemoglobin and hematocrit

explanation: Crossmatching is a crucial safety step! Lab staff mix donor cells and recipient serum together first to make sure they won't react violently inside the patient's body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: What does agglutination mean when performing a forward blood typing test?

options.A: The plasma separates completely from the solid blood components
options.B: The blood sample destroys itself due to lack of adequate nutrition
options.C: The red blood cells change their normal shape into sickle cells
options.D: The red blood cells clump together in the presence of matching antibodies

explanation: Agglutination is the visible clumping that occurs when antibodies bind to their specific matching antigens on red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is Type O-negative blood considered the universal red cell donor?

options.A: The blood type is the most common found in humans
options.B: The red blood cells lack A, B, and Rh antigens
options.C: The red blood cells have no hemoglobin inside them
options.D: The plasma contains high levels of protective platelets

explanation: Because Type O-negative red blood cells carry none of the major antigens, recipient antibodies have nothing to react against. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: A patient with Type AB-positive blood needs emergency red blood cells and none of their exact type is available. Which blood type can they safely receive?
explanation: Type AB-positive individuals are universal recipients for red blood cells because their blood does not contain antibodies against A, B, or Rh antigens. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is your very first nursing action if you suspect a transfusion reaction?

options.A: Increase the intravenous fluid flow rate
options.B: Collect a fresh blood sample for typing
options.C: Administer a dose of prescribed antihistamines

explanation: Patient safety first! Stopping the infusion right away prevents any more incompatible red blood cells from flowing into the patient. You'll master this clinical skill in no time! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Fever and severe lower back pain
options.B: Sudden drop in body temperature and shivering
options.C: Chest tightness and feeling of impending doom
options.D: Dark-colored urine caused by free hemoglobin

explanation: Watch out for trick questions like this! Transfusion reactions usually cause a fever, not a drop in temperature, along with back pain, dark urine, and anxiety. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)
